utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. It's Joanna Korner, Alex Demirdjian, Tijana Kaletovic, and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, Ms. Tatjana Savic, and Ms. Deirdre Montgomery appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. For the Defence of Mr. Zupljanin, Aleksandar Aleksic, Kieran Rigney, and Monica Feltz.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Your --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, with respect to the question of timing that I raised yesterday afternoon. I've spoken to Mr. Zecevic this morning, and I understand his revised -- his estimate as to how long he's going to be, and I think, perhaps, I'd better let him tell you. Your Honours, the only other suggestion I have is, as Your Honours will recall, when we were asked about timings, I suggested we should sit next week for the three days between Easter and the Queen's holiday, and as far as we're concerned, if that's possible with the Court, we could deal with cross-examinations, start this week, and go over until next week. It's the huge gap that we wouldn't want.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry. Yesterday I wasn't really accurate at all, because after I revised -- re-checked my notes and the documents, I saw that only one-third of the documents have been produced so far. So, therefore, I'm pretty sure that I would need all 20 hours, as suggested at the beginning. I'm sorry for creating this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Which more or less means that at the actual pace it will take next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure that not before Wednesday, but it depends how the situation develops, because this week we didn't -- the three days, I had only seven hours of direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic, did you wish to say something? I see you were getting to your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I just wished to add that Mr. Krgovic said that we would need an hour and a half. Perhaps his examination of this witness is going to be a bit shorter than that, but of course it depends on how the direct examination goes. So far, we stick to the original hour and a half. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So it seems to me that the pace at which we are moving is such that we need -- it would be imprudent to attempt to make any new decision now, and we would assess the situation, say, at the -- when we rise on Tuesday, perhaps. Yes. Could the Usher please -- if there are no other matters, could the Usher please escort the witness back to the stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Mr. Registrar, can I inquire whether the drawing is available, that we can deal with the map today? Thank you. A different courtroom today, so that's why I ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Bjelosevic. You may be seated. And before I invite Mr. Zecevic to resume his examination-in-chief, I remind you you're still on your oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I sit down now? I cannot hear any interpretation, you see.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The witness says he doesn't have the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, I can't hear it. I think it's all right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Can you hear me now? In which case I --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So I would remind you that you're still on your oath, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bjelosevic, could we please look at document 1D46, tab -- oh, I see, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Mr. Usher, can I ask you for ... [Interpretation] Tab 47. The document is 1D46.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, a few questions -- a few questions before we comment on this document. You have a degree in National Defence, a university degree; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think that you told us that for nine or ten years you worked at the Secretariat for National Defence.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Seven years.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: During the war, you said that you spent some time in the military. Tell me, do you hold some rank in the military?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1991, I was promoted to the rank of captain first class. That is my military rank. And at the end of the war, I was a colonel of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: However, at that time in 1992, there were no ranks in the police force; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In 1992, no. But later on they were introduced.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you said "captain first class," did you mean reserve captain first class?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, reserve captain first class. That is to say, I was not an active-duty officer; rather, I was a reserve captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, please take a look at the document in front of you. This is a document dated the 15th of May, 1992. It is an order signed by the minister of the interior, Mico Stanisic. Tell me, had you received this order in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mentioned that yesterday; this document, among others. That is what the members of Parliament brought to me from Pale when they attended the Assembly meeting there, when they flew on that helicopter. We received this document, this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Bjelosevic -- actually, could you give us your comments on paragraph 7 and 8 of this order? Tell us how you see them and understand them. That is page 2 of the document.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is being ordered here -- or, rather, what is being stated here is what should be done; namely, that the use of ministry units in co-ordinated actions with the armed forces can be ordered by the minister of the interior, the commander of the police detachment of the ministry, and the chief of the CSB. I have to note that at that point in time we did not have any communication whatsoever. I'm actually referring to May and June. This order dates back to May. We did not have any communication whatsoever with the minister or the ministry. However, this document was something that we went by. It was pointed out here that when carrying out combat actions the units of the ministry should be subordinated to the command of the armed forces; however, the ministry units shall be under the direct command of a designated ministry official. That was in accordance with the Law on Defence. And you can see here that the minister, himself, is observing the law and issuing instructions on that basis. Paragraph 8 speaks of regular duties and tasks. And what is called for is the strict observance of the Law on the Ministry of the Interior and other relevant regulations. And as for the military, military regulations and rules should be enforced, which is fully in accordance with the then relevant law.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just a few questions, if I may. Could you please explain to us what this means, because if I understood you correctly, you actually carried this out in practice. What does it mean when units of the ministry are under the direct command of designated officials from the ministry, in accordance with paragraph 7?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means that if the police was supposed to be used on the basis of an order, and we already said that the military commanders had the right to issue such orders, then a company is established. A commander of that company is appointed from the ranks of the police. However, such companies, together with their commanders, once they go out to carry out an assignment, they are under the command of a higher-ranking command, say a battalion. The battalion has its own command. However, again, they are subordinated to the higher military command whose tasks they carry out and whose organic structure they belong to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does that mean that the commander of that police unit - let's say it's a company - is then subordinated to the command of that battalion, part of which the unit had become?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. Let me try to be even clearer. I have already mentioned that a few times I was appointed commander, myself. For Operation Corridor, they established ad hoc troops for me. It was not a set wartime unit. There were four companies of the police, or "milicija," within it. Every company was headed by a commander who was a police officer. I also had a military police company, and this military police company had a commander of their own who was an officer. I also had two companies of the Krajina police. Every one of those companies had its own commander, and I was the commander of them all. However, I, as the commander of that formation, was subordinated to the command of the tactical group. That is to say that we all operated in accordance with plans and orders issued by Tactical Group 3 at that point in time. I assume that it is well known that the army is established according to the principle of subordination and singleness of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to invite you to comment upon the last part of the sentence in bullet point 8, where it says that military rules and regulations are applied in military operations. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bullet point 7 or 8?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Eight.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Any violation of regulations and failure to carry out tasks which have been ordered shall be subject to severe punishment ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, I meant the first paragraph in bullet point 8, the last sentence, where it says. "... whereas in military operations, military regulations and rules shall be enforced."

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was. From that moment when the police is deployed in combat, it represents an element of the armed forces and is subject to all rules and possible disciplinary measures applied by the military, because they are engaged in combat by the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now look at 1D406, tab 58.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that. The Command of the 1st Krajina Corps, Duga Njiva Forward Command Post, the same one that we talked about yesterday. This is a commander's order.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, before the 30th of June, did you spend some time at that forward command post in Duga Njiva?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Once -- when my combat force was dismantled, I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can we please look at page 2, the third and second paragraph from the bottom. And the sentence starts with: "The exclusive right of command ..."

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The zone commander shall have the exclusive right of command, as per this order. In the conduct of combat activities, all police forces shall be placed under the command of the zone commander, who shall decide how they are used." I'm absolutely clear about the contents of this document, and I believe that the order is clear. In the army, orders are usually formulated so as to be clear. It says here that the commander of the zone shall have the exclusive right to use the units in his zone. And it says here that all police forces shall be placed under the command of the zone commander, who shall decide how they are used. And this is also clear, and this is even more precise, and this is exactly how we operated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, was that in keeping with the regulations that were in effect at the time?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fully. Fully in compliance with the rules that were in effect at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at 1D -- D1552. That's tab 105.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this was sent on the 7th of September, 1992, by the command of Tactical Group 3. This is an order to attack. The order was signed by Colonel Slavko Lisica. Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I have the tab number again? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: 105, 105. 65 ter -- Defence 65 ter 552D1. It is the document that we have on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm familiar with this document because the Command of Tactical Group 3 regularly copied us with the orders that concerned the police. Sometimes they were sent in their integral form, sometimes in the form of excerpts. In any case, we received those orders regularly. Therefore, I am familiar with this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "to us," who do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean the centre and the public security stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I would like to invite your comment upon bullet point 5.2 or paragraph 5, bullet point 2.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Doboj police battalion is attacking, and then the topographic features are set out. Yes, an order is hereby issued by the police battalion to engage in attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me: Mr. Lisica, the commander of Tactical Group 3 at the time, was he also the commander of the zone?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Let's be very clear on this. Every unit is assigned its zone of responsibility. Tactical Group 3 was assigned its own zone of responsibility. Therefore, whatever was happening in the area of responsibility of Tactical Group 3 was within the purview of the command and the commander of that zone. In this case, they would be Tactical Group 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unless there are objections, I would like to tender the document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D468, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, can we now look at 196D1, tab 59. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document was issued on the 3rd of July, 1992. In the heading, you can see that it was drafted by the Ministry of the Interior, Security Services Centre Doboj. The typed-up signature is that of Andrija Bjelosevic. There is also a stamp. Is this your document? Can you confirm that this is your document, and can you also tell us what the document refers to?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document that I drafted, that I created. It bears a stamp and my signature. I signed it. And let me explain how the document came about and when it was drafted. On the 1st of July, I was injured and driven from Teslic to a hospital, and I signed this document in hospital. My associates paid me visits while I was in hospital. And since we had plenty of time to engage in discussions, we did that. I was under a strong impression of what I had seen and experienced in Teslic, and I talked with my associates about their own impressions with regard to the work of the police, and so on and so forth. And then I ordered them to go and inspect those units which were still units, not regulated police stations. That's how the police were deployed. And we could already get in contact with Modrica and Derventa. And they inspected all those areas, they collected information, and they put me abreast of the situation, so I could understand from that that the police did, indeed, act illegally, and the order is a result of that. I'm ordering the police to start the training regarding the use of authority, particularly regarding the use of force, and I also emphasised that the use of force had -- truncheons and fire-arms had to be used according to the rules. And I drew special attention to the conditions for the necessity to justify the use of force.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain how the use of force is justified in the Ministry of the Interior? What rules and regulations are used for that? How is that regulated?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was regulated by the law and the regulations that were both in force, and I'm referring to both of them in this order, the regulations on service in the enforcement agencies. That means that if the police issued an order and if that order was not obeyed by the person who was caught in committing crimes or they had already committed a crime and they are resisting arrest, then the use of force is in order, which can include restraining or the use of truncheons. And in the most drastic cases, when the lives of the police officers or other citizens were at risk, in keeping with those regulations, the police officer had the right to use fire-arms. If only physical force was used, then, obviously, police officers had to write a report about the physical force having been used, when it was used, and why, and that report was read and taken under the advisement by the chief of the police station. If other means of force were used, like, for example, truncheons or, God forbid, fire-arms, then the police officers who had used those had to report to the chief of the Security Services Centre. The policeman would write a report, the report would then be inspected first by the commander of his police station, and then the report would be sent to the chief of the Security Services Centre. When the report was put in the context of the prevailing regulations, he could judge whether the use of force had been justified or not. In practice, I encountered both situations. In Petrovo, in my view, the use of fire-arms was not justified, and that policeman who used fire-arms was sentenced to a prison sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You have given us an example in your last sentence. If you, as the chief of the Security Services Centre, deemed that the use of force or additional forms, including fire-arms, was not justified, what measures could be taken?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A criminal report is filed against the policeman who used that force and sent to an investigating judge, because at that time in 1992, investigations were conducted by investigative judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And what about the Ministry of the Interior; were measures taken by the ministry or not? I'm talking about disciplinary measures.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. When criminal proceedings were initiated, the subject of those criminal proceedings would be suspended until the end of those criminal proceedings. If the person was found guilty and charged, then the measure would be pronounced. And if he was acquitted, in that case his job would be reinstated and he would suffer no other consequences or disciplinary measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please comment on the penultimate sentence of the document. It concerns who this order shall not be applied to.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not supposed to be applied to those parts of the police which were included in immediate combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us why this was inserted in your order and for what reason?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the reason was already explained, but I will repeat. The police, if used in the exercise of combat tasks, it was re-subordinated to the army and respective military commands. It was considered part of the armed forces, and military regulations were applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There seems to be a problem with the translation of this document. The CLSS translation seems to be faulty.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please read out that sentence slowly from the document.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "This order shall not apply to parts of the police which are involved in actual war operations."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Looking at the English translation, the double negative was somewhat confusing, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's obviously a mistake, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So I suppose the document should be referred back to CLSS for --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is what I intend to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. If there is no objection, I seek to tender this document; MFI'd, though, pending a revised translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I said yesterday, in order to prevent me having to get up each time and ask whether this was a document provided by this witness, I could be provided with a list. I was told I would be. I haven't been yet. Am I going to be provided with a list?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I thought it was already done, because I gave the instructions that the whole list will be provided to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I was told that this document is both from the disclosure from the Office of the Prosecutor and we received it from the witness as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So it's marked for identification, pending the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D469, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at 5531D. That is tab 106. It is a document of the Command of the Tactical Group 3, dated the 8th of September, 1992, signed by Colonel Lisica, commander, at least his name appears in the signature block.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether you are familiar with this order and what it pertains to?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with this order by Commander Lisica. As usual, military orders are clear, and so is this one. The commander, or the TG-3 Command, introduces military administration in the municipality of Derventa. Military organs' orders are the only orders to be implemented. Prior to this document, there already had been a military administration in Derventa, but the commander, if I recall correctly, was Jankovic, I believe. Here we have another person being appointed, which is Captain First Class Pero Stojakovic. I think the order is perfectly clear. And it is legitimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you clarify what such an introduction of a military administration means, or setting up a town command, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By way of introducing a military administration, a town commander is appointed, as we can see here when Captain First Class Pero Stojakovic was appointed. And he, in turn, chooses a number of associates of his to help him with the exercise of his duties in respect of fields or areas. As the order mentions, the command decides on a whole range of things, meaning the commander is in charge and there is a military administration in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say that they decide on a range of things or they decide about everything, can you be more precise?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can clearly see that in item 3. It reads: "The commander of the defence of Derventa is responsible for and has the duty to regulate, together with his organs, life and work, and everyone is expected to comply with his orders and instructions." There seems to be a grammatical error, but in any case, his instructions. It is as it says. This includes the entire population, and he was in charge of organising life and work in the area. If I may, I wish to remind the Chamber, or perhaps help them understand the situation better, of something that one needs to bear in mind. Part of the municipality of Derventa was still at war. It had not been liberated by that time. And the town had been destroyed and parts of it set ablaze. The infrastructure was in ruin, and people were trying to get back to their homes. It was a situation of chaos. That is why the commander decided to introduce a military administration, in order to deal with the situation as efficiently as possible, so that people would not return any which way and that chaos would not prevail.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Such an introduction of a military administration, what impact, if any, does it have on the work of the police and the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Officially speaking, there had already been a public security station in Derventa by that time. The building where it was housed was torched. Only the walls were left, and the rest was destroyed, including all the documents. For the initial period of time, the police station was situated in the local primary school, and later on it was transferred to the Institute for the Blind. Basically, they started from scratch, although they did have a number of personnel. On top of that, Commander Lisica issued an order by which he sent all police personnel from Derventa to combat. By virtue of this same order, he introduced a police force from Prnjavor, and he tasked them with policing in the town itself. He justified that decision by his need to -- of the Derventa population to gain greater confidence in the Derventa police force, and that is why he said he sent them to combat, because he believed they would enjoy greater respect with the population once they returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there is no objection, I seek to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: This relates exclusively to Derventa. Why should it be exhibited?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: To save -- Your Honours, we don't object, and we say we can see it's relevant, and we're going to be dealing with it. In fact, I think it came in in an earlier -- under an earlier witness, at some stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D470 [Realtime transcript read in error "170"], Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think the number should be 1D470.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It was recorded something differently in the transcript. I'm sorry. [Interpretation] Could we look at 1D407, MFI, which is tab 109.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, in this document it says "Security Services Centre Doboj." The date is the 10th of September, 1992, and in the signature block we see "Andrija Bjelosevic," with a stamp and signature. Can you confirm whether this is your document and what it pertains to?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I signed it and sent it to the public security stations. If you look at the introduction, you can conclude what it has to do with. It was issued based on an order of the operational group. By this time, the situation was somewhat improved in the area, although I must repeat that still the situation was quite chaotic. There were masses of exiled population, people moving about in uniform, thousands upon thousands of refugees. They arrived in uniform, with weapons, looking for a place to stay for themselves and their families. The front-lines were in immediate vicinity, and the area was daily shelled by enemy artillery. Those people who came in uniform resembled members of the army, whereas many of them did not belong to any military units. They were trying or looking for ways to deal with their own refugee situation. In doing so, they frequently resorted to violence. They looked for goods, something that they could live on. They looked for a place for their family to stay. Once we diagnosed the problem, stronger controls were required in order to have all the people moving about in uniform who were not members of certain units and those who did not have their wartime disposition and who were not on leave, to have their uniforms taken away, seized, and returned. That is why we ordered more stringent controls at check-points.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your clarification. I can see that the document speaks for itself. I'm interested in the introduction. We see that the order of the operational group is attached. Since you were forwarding that order, did you expect the public security stations to implement that operational group order? And if so, on what basis?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the basis of order-issuing authority, on the basis of the fact that it is the area of responsibility of the command that had issued the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document not be marked for identification any longer, because the previous witness could not deal with it, the previous witness who it had been shown to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we would remove the MFI qualification.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, just for the record, this is Exhibit 1D407.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2291D [as interpreted]; that is, tab 127. Could we please have a look at that document. Could we please have page 2. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, this is a document of the Doboj CSB. The date is the 21st of September, 1992. It is sent to the Command of the Operations Group of the Serb Army in Doboj. On the third page, we see the name of "Andrija Bjelosevic, Chief of Centre," typed out, and we see a signature. Can you confirm for us, Mr. Bjelosevic, that this is your document, and can you please explain what this is all about? Can you explain what it is that you were asking for by way of this document?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document was signed by me; that is to say, I signed this document. It is sent to the Command of the Operations Group of Doboj. And we are asking for certain persons, those listed under numbers 1 through 14, to be freed from the military and sent to a course for police training that was organised from the 21st of September, 1992, onwards. As far as I can remember, the command allowed us to do this, and they freed these persons so that they could attend the course. The Public Security Station of Maglaj was in Jablanica, and that is where this happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, there is a reference to these 14 candidates here, and it says at the moment they are in the Serbian Army. These 14 candidates, were they reserve policemen?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were reserve policemen among them, but there were also others who were subsequently asked for within this number but who had not been policemen to begin with. So there were both.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry, that was a horribly leading question, because it's exactly the point that needed to be clarified by way of a non-leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. My mistake. It's to my own detriment, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, if some persons who are members of the police are serving in the military at a given point in time, what possibilities do you have, as chief of the CSB, in relation to such persons?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a situation that we had in the territory of several police stations; Derventa, among others. I am pointing it out with good reason, because the entire police personnel in Derventa at one point in time quite literally joined the army. They were re-subordinated to the army. As a matter of fact, they didn't even operate as a separate unit, headed by their own commander. They were deployed in different units. Some were deployed in the scouts units, some in the military police, some were -- well, the military police also had a crime investigation department, so some of them were deployed there too. When Derventa was liberated, when the Public Security Station there was established, there were major problems involved in order to have the command allow us to enable all the policemen to return to the Public Security Station. They did not have sufficient personnel either, so little by little they let them go, they let them return to the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And what were your possibilities in terms of reacting to that situation?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could write, asking for them to be freed from the military and asking for approval to be given for them to return to the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you say "I could write," or did you say that you could not write?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I could write. I could write and ask for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at 556D1, tab 128.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you want that exhibited?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I thought that you, Ms. Korner, would object. Well, if not, then I would gladly have that exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D471, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, 65 ter Defence 229D1 is 1D471. Thank you. [Interpretation] 556D1, could we have that document, please, tab 128A.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, yet again, this is an order of the command of Tactical Group 3 from Banja Luka on the 23rd of September, 1992. On page 2, there is a signature of the commander, Colonel Lisica. Since this is a copy from a book, there is another document that follows after this one. Are you familiar with this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is an order for further combat operations. And it is clear from this order that this task was being issued to the combat group of the police, the "milicija" as well, that was engaged under the command of Tactical Group 3. It acted in concert with the brigade --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the name of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the name of the brigade because the interpreters did not hear you.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not brigade. This actually means "combat group." Combat group. Combat group. So the equivalent would not be the strength of a brigade, but it would be a combat group.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, it says here "in concert or in co-ordination with a brigade."

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I see, the Osinja Brigade; that's what you meant. The brigade was named after a town called Osinja, and that is why it is called the Osinja Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Since there is a reference here to co-ordinated action, acting in concert, can you briefly explain this word to us, what this co-ordinated action means as a military term, and whether certain prerequisites had to be met in order to have co-ordinated action?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that means acting together, carrying out a task together, acting in concert together, carrying out a task by way of co-ordinated action.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: A specific question -- let me put a specific question to you now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] In a non-leading form.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The authority that is issuing an order related to co-ordinated action, what should be the relationship between that order-issuing authority and the units that the order is being issued to?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the commanding order-issuing authority for the units to whom or to which the order is being issued for co-ordinated action. Well, it depends. It depends on the territory involved. If the territory is cut up, in a way, if there are barriers of any kind, artificial, man-made, or natural barriers, and if different units are being engaged, nevertheless, these units have to act under a single command, in concert, so that a single objective could be attained. I would like to underline that this is something that probably exists in all armies worldwide. Singleness of command and unity of command are a prevailing principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I see number 3 here. It says "Combat Group Mesa Selimovic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. Mr. Witness, in co-ordinated action, such a co-ordinated action, is that the same as re-subordination? Does this mean that the police combat group was re-subordinated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now there were three questions there, and could I please be allowed to explain that. Re-subordination is something that goes without saying by virtue of the fact that one comes and is made available to a particular command. That means that re-subordination has already taken place. Then you refer to the word "co-ordination." This word "koordinacija" does not work in the army, whereas "sadejstvo," as "co-ordination," does. So when a commander has subordinates within the combat order, then he issues orders to them and then says what the elements involved are for co-ordinated action. It's not that one unit is given just one task.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I may be of assistance, Your Honours. I believe there was a problem with the -- in the terms, because during the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please take off your headphones. [In English] During the examination of a military expert, we had the same problem of translating the word "sadejstvo," and I believe it was concluded at the end, with the help of the interpreters, that "sadejstvo" should be interpreted as "co-ordinated action." And that is the term that is used in this Tribunal, because "sadejstvo" is one thing and "koordinacija," "co-ordination," is the other. So in order to distinct between the two, we -- let me remind you that we agreed that "sadejstvo" would be translated always as "co-ordinated action," whereas "co-ordination" will be translated -- or "koordinacija," will be translated as "co-ordination." And I believe that might be the reason, according to my understanding of the witness's answer, why he's -- because he said the co-ordination does not exist in the military, and I believe, Your Honour, meant the actual word which was used in the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I'm still -- no, no. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I'm still not completely sure, Mr. Bjelosevic. This order is about two groups, the police combat group and the Osinja Brigade - the brigade is obviously military - and asks -- or orders them to work together; right? Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, they are ordered to carry out a particular task involving co-ordinated action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Now, my question is: As far as the police brigade concerns -- the police combat group, sorry, the police combat group is concerned, is this order addressed/given to a police combat group that previously was re-subordinated or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me try and explain things in a more plastic [as interpreted] way. Let's be clear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just, could you first, if possible, give me a yes or no and then explain? Was this order given to a police combat group that was previously re-subordinated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's make things very clear. Let's see how things looked on the ground. In the military and in military units, there are several ways how units work in combat. One unit can be given a task on its own. The unit is given an axis of action, and they execute the task on its own. That unit may be reinforced by different means. And if that happens, then the unit is expanded. Also, the superior command can add a certain unit, or a group, to that original unit or attach another unit, and then they act in concert. However, both units are subordinated to that higher command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I suppose we may as well take the break at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: There is something I neglected to do at the beginning and that is to note for the record that today, again, we convene under Rule 15 bis, Judge Harhoff being absent. So we would return in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, while the witness is ushered, I would just like to inform the Trial Chamber of two things. I was informed by the Registry, and I'm very thankful for that, that the map got recovered, the map which was drawn yesterday by Mr. -- by our witness, Mr. Bjelosevic, and so I would suggest that the Registry just repeats the number, for the record, of that exhibit so we can have it admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That was Exhibit 1D462, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And the -- thank you, Your Honours. And the second thing is: I was advised that 1D460, which was MFI'd yesterday, we received a revised translation, and request the MFI be removed from the -- it was up-loaded, the new translation has been up-loaded, and we request that the MFI be removed from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So ordered.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I continue? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bjelosevic, we're still talking about the same document, 556D1, tab 128A.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [In English] I'm sorry, Your Honours. I was inquiring whether Your Honours want me to pursue the questions Your Honour asked or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] We're satisfied.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You're satisfied. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one clarification, if you can. Under 3: "BG, Mesa Selimovic BG"?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Since Mr. Mesa Selimovic was a well-known writer, Bosnian writer I should say, and a member of the Muslim ethnicity, I would like to know --

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean how come that he is -- his name has found its place in the military?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, among the Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This "BG" was established and soon became a company. It was a unit which was mostly composed of Bosniaks and some Croats. When that unit was established, although it was not very customary at the time, they went to see Commander Lisica and asked him to be the godfather of their unit, and he gave it the name Mesa Selimovic, and they kept the name until the end of the war. Later on, they became part of the 327th Brigade. They were volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unless there are objections, I would like to tender the document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D472, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look at 560D1, under tab 141.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, yet again, this is an order issued by TG-3 on the 7th October, 1992. On the second page, the order was signed by Colonel Slavko Lisica, who was the commander of that group. There is a stamp and a signature there. I would like to know whether you're familiar with this order. And I'm especially interested in paragraphs 1(c) and (d). This is an order. It has several bullet points. Could you please comment upon it.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with this order by Commander Lisica. When Brod was liberated, that order was issued on the same day, on the 7th of October, 1992. You can see that military administration is being introduced, and the person who was appointed the commander of the city is Lieutenant-Colonel Mikic, and also a deputy is appointed. And Commander Lisica, as you can see, issues this order to establish a public security station, and he is the one who appoints who the chief of the Public Security Station would be. It would be Nenad Milicic, who up to then was the commander of the Brod Battalion. He also appoints his deputy the chief of the station. It did not exist under the establishment, but since the commander established the Public Security Station, he also appoints personnel and organises its structure. And further on in his order, the commander elaborates how people should behave within the organisation that he established. Most interesting of all this, bullet point 4, where it says that: "All appointed organs and individuals shall be subordinated to the town commander."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unless there are objections, I would like to tender the document into evidence. I know that this document concerns Bosanski Brod, but it illustrates the authorities of the TG commander with regard to all civilian organs, and that's why I believe that this document is also relevant for these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I accept that. My objections so far have been to leading evidence about events, and the like, outside the area. For the purposes for which Mr. Zecevic wishes to put it in, namely, to show their theory of the relationship between the military and the police, I accept that documents such as this are admissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D473, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: As a matter of curiosity, though, Mr. Zecevic: Of the number of documents which you've indicated you propose to tender, how many of them are merely illustrative? That wasn't a question inviting an answer. It was merely an observation that at some point the utility of these merely illustrative documents would cease to have any purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm glad to inform Your Honours that this is my last document which is of that illustrative nature concerning this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So noted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, could you please look at 245D1, tab 158. The document was issued on the 3rd of November, 1992. I believe that it is a dispatch which was delivered to the MUP of the Republika Srpska. The signatory is "Chief of Centre, Andrija Bjelosevic." There is a signature. Can you please just confirm for us whether this is, indeed, your document, and what does it refer to?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. There is something added by hand, so I would like to invite your comment with this regard. Who was it who added the words in hand?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a dispatch that I sent, and this is information for the ministry about what had happened. Nenad Milicic was appointing the chief of the Bosanski Brod Station by Commander Lisica, as we've just seen, was found in Doboj, and he was in the process of stealing, together with some other uniform personnel from Bosanski Brod, and they were robbing a house. The family of Nenad Milicic was housed there while they were displaced. They had all fled Brod. And then on their way back to Brod -- or, rather, when they returned to Brod, they repaired their house, they made it possible to live in, and then he and a group of his associates went back to the house where they had stayed as displaced persons in order to take the household items and bring them back to Bosanski Brod and furnish his house there. With all due understanding for the hardships of the Milicic family, there was certainly no way to procure household items for their own goods. The police intervened, they prevented them in carrying on that activity, and then Colonel Lisica, who had been informed, and Milicic was within his authority, Colonel Lisica reassigned him to a duty in Benkovac. And I proposed somebody else to perform the duties as the chief of the Public Security Station. My proposal was subsequently accepted, and the person was, indeed, appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When did that proposal of yours arrive?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Immediately following this event. I can't recall the date, but it was as soon as I had agreed with Commander Lisica that the Public Security Station ought to be made part of the Security Centre of the ministry. That is when I initiated that proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that was the gist of my question, which was whether, at the moment when you made that proposal for appointment of a new chief of the Public Security Station in Bosanski Brod, the Military Administration was then abolished. In other words, what happened with the command in the town?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Military Administration stayed in place. But since Commander Lisica and I had discussed the situation, I successfully managed to argue my position that the security station should be within the ministry hierarchy, just under the Security Centre. And I told him that in that way we would be able to control the situation. He agreed for the station to start operating as a proper public security station outside the structure which was under the town command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You say that Colonel Lisica agreed. Had he not, would you have been able to --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I was about to rise to my feet to object to the leading question before that as well, because the question that Mr. Zecevic said that he asked was that the gist of his question, which was not the gist of his question, and in the form in which it was asked is leading, the way this question is going to be asked now is also a leading one. So before he can ask it, I'm objecting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm withdrawing. Thank you very much, Ms. Korner. Your Honours, I misspoke. This document -- I called this document by our 65 ter Defence number, but I was reminded that this document is already in exhibits as 1D408, and it was MFI'd because the previous witness couldn't authorise the document. Now, Mr. Bjelosevic confirmed that this is his document, and I propose that this document be de-MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, so ordered.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 1D410, which is tab 167. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is an operational group document, signed by Commander Colonel Slavko Lisica. The date is the 11th of November, 1992. It is an order. In item 2, there is a reference -- your name appears, that is. Could you please comment.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me say, briefly, that following the liberation of the Posavina area, Commander Lisica was appointed commander of the operational group in Doboj. Here, we can see it mentioned. I am familiar with the order. The command planned for certain combat tasks to be executed. In item 1, it says: "Form a mixed battalion ..." Et cetera. And you can see that, again, this formation was an ad hoc formation with the company of the military police and a company of the regular police. I don't recall how many companies there were exactly, but Teslic is also mentioned. I am being appointed battalion commander by virtue of this order. He also decided on my deputy. And in item 3, he mentions certain elements of combat readiness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you abide by this order by Commander Lisica?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bjelosevic, let us move on to another topic. But, first of all, let me ask you something. What was the situation like in Doboj in 1992, and how far was Doboj from the separation line or the front-line? What consequence did it have for the people living in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war, that area, together with the area that is westwards towards Krajina, had been surrounded completely. There was no traffic, the economy was in shambles, and there was no possibility of supply. Just to illustrate that, I will remind you that in the Banja Luka Clinical Centre, 12 babies died because there was no oxygen that could be provided to them. So the area was encircled. The proximity of the front-line to the east went along the Bosna River, which is right next to the urban settlement, the town itself. To the south, there was the Bosna and the Usora. Therefore, it was adjacent to the front-line. The situation was chaotic because the front-lines were so close and because the area was exposed to enemy artillery fire. There were thousands of refugees from different places as well, and I have already mentioned that there were many uniformed and armed people moving about. When the JNA withdrew, certain groups and even units ran amok. They were no longer under the unified command, and acted as paramilitary structures. I believe I can freely say that the Doboj population was terrorised during that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say that the population was terrorised, who do you have in mind? Who was terrorising them?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The paramilitary groups I just mentioned, as well as individuals. There were also people who were refugees who recognised no orders or commands. They took it upon themselves to find accommodation for them and to provide for themselves, even if it meant appropriating other people's property, breaking into other people's homes, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: As the chief of the Security Centre, did you take any measures against such behaviour?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We always took measures. Whenever we received information of such events, we established an on-site investigation team which attended the scenes of crimes, upon which a prosecutor and an investigative judge were always informed. Documentation was filed and case files opened alongside investigations. Of course, there were instances when perpetrators were identified and proceedings instituted, but some crimes had not been resolved during my stay there. In other words, the perpetrators were not found.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, was Doboj town and the municipality shelled from positions held by Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, almost daily. There were numerous reports about that. I think there were 94 civilian casualties as a result of that, including people of different age, such as children, women, men, and people of different ethnicities among the victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'll show a document, which is 267D1, tab 187, and I'd like you to comment. It's a dispatch from the CSB Doboj to the RS MUP on the 27th of November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is a dispatch sent to the Ministry of the Interior. It was supposed to inform them of what was going on. We were under an obligation to provide such information for their bulletin. We can see that on the 26th of November there was shelling in town, causing property damage. Then in Samac, the situation was similar, which is something we can see in the next paragraph, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The victims in Samac are enumerated in paragraph 2. If we look at the names, can you tell us what their nationality was, what was their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I certainly can. They were Muslim, Mustafa and Zeina Kapetanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This dispatch was sent from the CSB, on your behalf, to the RR MUP; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there is no objection, I seek to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'd like to know about the handwriting, please, and where it comes from, this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you comment on the handwritten annotations, since I am not allowed to do that, in the right-hand side corner in the top.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is a signature which I don't recognise, and the date is when it was received and processed so as to include it in the information bulletin issued by the minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you read what it says.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Analysis Department, it was forwarded to them. They gathered and collated all the information included in the information bulletin. That is to say, they had field information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise the handwriting?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. My second question was: Where does the document come from?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think it's a batch -- I have here it's a batch 170, document 70, so that's a disclosure from the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D474, [Realtime transcript read in error "470"], Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I believe we passed the number 470.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I think I said "474," just to correct the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to show you another document, 260D1, tab 180. It's also a dispatch of the CSB Doboj, sent to the MUP of Republika Srpska on the 23rd of November, 1992. Your name is typewritten at the bottom of the page, in your capacity of chief of centre?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is information provided to the ministry. It has to do with the following event: "On the 23rd of November, 1992, between 1100 and 1410 hours, five shells fell on the area of the town of Doboj, causing severe injuries to six persons and killing a child." Again, you can see that it is being sent to the Analysis Department, so it's taking the same path, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a document that was disclosed by the Prosecutor, batch 170, and it was number 68. If there are no objections, I would like to tender this document as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D475, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. I keep forgetting that I switch off the microphone, as instructed by interpreters, because I'm shuffling the papers and they can't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since we are discussing Doboj now, I'm going to go back to that and I'm going to ask you about some facts that were proffered here by the Prosecution and accepted by the Trial Chamber. Tell me -- I think that we discussed this on the first day. We discussed check-points that were put up in the territory of Doboj. Tell me, when were these check-points put up in the area of the town of Doboj, who kept these check-points, who manned them, and until when?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please be more specific? When you say "the territory of Doboj," do you mean the territory of the municipality or the check-points in town? I spoke about check-points that were placed in the surrounding area. That is also the territory of Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let me just explain: In town and in the territory of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both. Check-points in the territory of the municipality were put up by different forces as far back as March. I, myself, came across a check-point once in the village of Jekovac [phoen]. It was manned by HDZ forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you give us the month, could you please provide the year as well?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1992. Also, now was this the end of month or the beginning of April? In the territory of the municipality of Doboj Istok, check-points were put up as well, and weapons were seized from JNA members when they arrived there. Vehicles were also taken. There were such check-points in other places as well; around Modrica and Derventa too, I think. But let's go back to Doboj. It is precisely because of such occurrences that the Council for National Defence of the municipality of Doboj, together with the commander of the Doboj Garrison, Colonel Cazim Hadzic, and the representatives of the police, all agreed that check-points manned by joint teams should be established within the town of Doboj, itself, that would keep the situation stable and under control. In addition to that, in the area towards Susnjari, where Gradina is in Doboj, and further on, there were check-points there as well. People could not enter the area whenever they wanted to. Even the police, the "milicija," could not enter unannounced. And everyone knew who could get in and when.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: These last check-points where the police could not enter unannounced, who manned these check-points?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These units are under the command of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, when you say "the Council for the National Defence of the municipality of Doboj," did that body consist of representatives of all the national parties or was this something different?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The council was made up of certain officials. Ahmet Alicic, president of the municipality, was a member ex officio; then the president of the Executive Council, I think it was Boro Paravac; then the secretary of National Defence; then the commander of the garrison; and the representative of the MUP. So it didn't really have to do with persons' names. The MUP was always represented by someone at these sessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, this organ was a multi-ethnic one, if I can put it that way?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, it was multi-ethnic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the Trial Chamber, this is an adjudicated fact; 1265 is the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, were you present at the last session of the Municipal Assembly of Doboj in 1992, the last joint session of the municipality of Doboj, and could you please tell us when that happened?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember when the session of the Municipal Assembly was held, and I was not present.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what was discussed at this session of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was certain basic issues that we had information about that were dealt with. I think that what was discussed was the division of the municipality. I don't know whether it was the last session, but, anyway, at one of the sessions that is what was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the result was of the political agreement?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, something was agreed upon, after all. However, I'm not familiar with the details, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "agreed upon," do you mean in relation to what was discussed about the division of the municipality, or something different?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The division of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is Adjudicated Fact 1266. 1266.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, do you know about the arrival of a large group of paramilitaries, if I can put it that way, or the White Eagles, in the territory of the municipality? If so, can you tell us when that occurred? Do you have any information to the effect that it happened in the beginning of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. To the best of my knowledge, there was no such formation in the territory of the municipality of Doboj. A smaller group, although they weren't called the White Eagles either, that could be reminiscent of that was Luis's Group that was in the territory of the municipality of Modrica. In the area of the municipality of Doboj, there were no such forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Zecevic. You may want to correct the spelling of "Luis" on the screen. Page 43, line 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think it's been corrected already.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's still wrong, but never mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I can make the reference to the exhibit before, but I think it's not needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bjelosevic, we have already seen how many members this group, Luis's Group, had. Now I'm going to ask you about the following fact: Do you know that a group of about 500 men, members of the White Eagles, arrived in the municipality of Doboj in January and February of 1992 and that they came to the Doboj Military Barracks to take lunch, to have dinner, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have never received such information. I have never heard of any such thing having happened. If a formulation like that had arrived in Doboj, people would have to know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "people would have to know about it," I assume that the police would have to know that a big group like that had come to the territory of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, imagine a formation of 500 men. It wouldn't only be the police; it would be generally well known. Five hundred men is a battalion, a strong battalion at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, do you know of an area close to Doboj that is called Ankara or Ankaran or something like that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a hill called Ankaran above Doboj. And there were repeaters there, different ones used for different purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "repeaters," you are referring to communications equipment; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Communications repeaters, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there was a group of people on that hill, Ankaran, that they had taken over that hill and forced the inhabitants from the area to move out? Are you aware of any such thing having happened?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is Adjudicated Fact 1267, for your reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, you told us about the situation on the 3rd of May, 1992. I think you also said that you had scheduled a meeting of the collegium.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to schedule it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And this collegium meeting was not held. Why not?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't possible to get all the personnel there, all the persons who made up the collegium of the chief of the centre. They did not respond to telephone calls.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The members of this collegium, or the members of the MUP who made up that collegium, were they ethnic Muslims and Croats and Serbs, that is to say, belonging to all three ethnic groups or peoples?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think I spoke about the ethnic composition over these past few days. It was heterogeneous, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: As for policemen who were ethnic Muslims, were any of them arrested on the 3rd of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. During the night, when the town was taken over, and the police building too, I think that the operations officers were there, were taken prisoner by the military. Yes, yes, taken prisoner, arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And what about all the other members of the police who were ethnic Muslims; were they arrested on or around the 3rd of May in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When the building was being taken over, the persons who happened to be there were. As for everybody being arrested, or, I don't know, whatever you said in your question, no, that was not the case. And the police were not all there in a single place, so it was not possible for that kind of thing to happen. I'm trying to say that even if somebody had wanted to do that, it was simply impossible to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge to the effect that perhaps there were individual arrests of such persons because they were members of the police; ethnic Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to what happened subsequently, who was brought in and why, I don't know well, for well-known reasons. I was not there all the time. And also at that time I did not deal with arrests and custody cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you know that a curfew was introduced in Doboj? If so, what do you know about it?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a curfew was, indeed, introduced about that time. The curfew was introduced by the Crisis Staff. I believe that it was primarily introduced for the safety of the citizens. That, at least, was the explanation that I heard. The safety of the citizens was at risk from shelling. The curfew was applied to all citizens, and the police controlled the implementation of the curfew.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, when were citizens allowed to move around the city?
